subtitle: Protocol for controlling switches and managing label-based forwarding in MPLS networks.

tldr.problem: Service providers need to control and manage switches separately from the routing control plane, to allow flexibility in hardware, enable multi-vendor networks, and support dynamic service provisioning.
tldr.mechanism: GSMP provides a master-slave protocol where a controller commands a switch to establish connections, configure ports, manage resources, and report statistics. The switch can run independently from routing protocols like BGP.
tldr.outcome: Operators can separate the control plane from the data plane, mix equipment from different vendors, and add services dynamically. GSMP v3 supports various switch types beyond ATM.

today: RFC 3294 is an informational document describing GSMP v3 applicability. GSMP remains an optional component in MPLS deployments, used where operators need explicit switch control rather than relying on interior gateway protocols for both routing and forwarding decisions.

sections.title: Overview and Purpose
sections.content:
The General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP) has evolved from a protocol designed for ATM switches to a general-purpose protocol for controlling label switches in IP and MPLS networks. GSMP v3 separates the data forwarding plane from the control plane: a controller sends commands to a switch to establish connections, manage ports, reserve resources, and request statistics. The switch responds with acknowledgments and can also send asynchronous event notifications, such as link state changes.

The protocol enables service providers to move away from monolithic systems that tightly couple control and forwarding. Instead, operators can deploy switches from one vendor controlled by routing software from another, allowing multi-vendor networks and greater operational flexibility. The Multiservice Switching Forum (MSF) selected GSMP as its protocol of choice for switch control interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of having one big box that does everything, you can have simple switches controlled by separate software. That lets you mix and match equipment from different companies.

sections.title: Switch Architecture and Label Types
sections.content:
A label switch is a frame or cell switch that uses exact-match forwarding on labels attached to incoming frames or cells. GSMP treats each switch (or virtual partition of a physical switch) as a collection of ports, where each port supports one label type. Label types supported include ATM VCs, Frame Relay DLCIs, DS1/DS3 circuits, MPLS generic labels, and MPLS Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs).

Connections are formed by connecting incoming labeled channels on an input port to one or more outgoing labeled channels on output ports. GSMP supports point-to-point connections (unicast), point-to-multipoint connections (one sender, multiple receivers), and approximations of multipoint-to-point and multipoint-to-multipoint. A single controller can manage multiple switches, and multiple controllers can manage a single switch for redundancy and load sharing, though coordination among controllers is the controllers' responsibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch has ports, each marked with a label. Connections link an input port label to output port labels, just like wires in a patch panel.

sections.title: Connections and Quality of Service
sections.content:
When the controller establishes a connection, it specifies the input port and label, the output port(s) and label(s), and a quality-of-service (QoS) class. GSMP v3 includes a default QoS configuration with three service models. The Service Model assigns a service type (from external definitions like CR-LDP or IntServ) that determines how the switch handles the connection. The Simple Priority Model assigns a priority level, and the switch favors higher-priority traffic when cells or frames share an output port. The QoS Profile Model allows a predefined profile identifier that encodes QoS semantics known to both controller and switch.

GSMP also supports resource reservation before labels are known, useful for MPLS deployments where label assignment may be dynamic. The controller can reserve bandwidth on ports and request statistics such as connection activity, port statistics, and per-connection statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: When you make a connection, you say how important it is. The switch then makes sure important connections get through even when it is busy.

sections.title: Messages and Protocol Operation
sections.content:
GSMP v3 defines several message categories. Connection Management Messages add or delete branches on point-to-point or multipoint connections, move branches, and delete entire connection trees. Port Management Messages configure ports and label ranges. Configuration Messages report and set switch and service configurations. Reservation Messages reserve and release switch resources. State and Statistics Messages request connection states and statistics. Event Messages notify the controller of asynchronous events like port up, port down, or invalid label errors.

The protocol operates over IP networks (using TCP), ATM virtual channels, or Ethernet links. An Adjacency Protocol synchronizes state, negotiates protocol version, discovers the entity on the other end of the link, and detects when it changes. A partition identifier carried in every message allows a physical switch to be sliced into virtual switches, each with its own controller.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller and switch exchange messages: 'add this connection,' 'delete that port,' 'send me statistics,' 'your link just went down.'

sections.title: Deployment in MPLS Networks
sections.content:
GSMP v3 is designed to work in MPLS networks where routing protocols and label distribution protocols (such as LDP or CR-LDP) run on a controller or control plane, while a separate label switch physically forwards packets. The controller uses GSMP to manage the switch, configure ports, and direct label distribution. This separation of concerns allows the switch to be a simpler, faster device.

In a typical deployment, a controller establishes BGP or other routing relationships and uses LDP to negotiate labels with other routers. When paths need to be set up, the controller uses GSMP to instruct the switch to create the forwarding rules. The switch can support multiple QoS configurations, and controllers can negotiate which QoS model the switch should use for a given connection or service.
sections.plainLanguage: The routing brain (controller) decides what connections to make. It tells the fast switch (data plane) exactly what to do via GSMP.
